articles.title: Philippine island fights rising seas with nature, not concrete
articles.summary: For years, residents of a flood-prone Philippine island north of Manila have elevated their homes atop layer upon layer of concrete, only to see floodwaters threaten them again.

blocks.text: For years, residents of a flood-prone Philippine island north of Manila have elevated their homes atop layer upon layer of concrete, only to see floodwaters threaten them again.

Burdened by strong storm surges, land subsidence and rising seas exacerbated by climate change, the 3,000 residents of tiny Pamarawan Island have turned to bamboo poles and discarded oyster shells to build a barrier aimed at weakening waves and managing floods.

The unusual approach offers a nature-based alternative for a country still grappling with a multibillion-dollar scandal that drove public fury over substandard — and at times non-existent — concrete flood-control projects.

"We were terrified whenever there were typhoons. We couldn't sleep at night," fisherman Edgar Javier told AFP on a recent visit, recalling how strong waves once brought down one of his home's concrete walls.
"Whenever the waves hit, the wall shakes."
The project began when the city government of Malolos, home to the island, launched a study with a Dutch engineering consultancy.
"(Concrete infrastructure) projects won't suffice," Mayor Christian Natividad told AFP.
While the project, the first of its kind in the country, initially faced resistance from officials and residents working without a blueprint, Natividad said they had "nothing to lose".
"It's like you accept daily flooding or you do something else with risk," he said.
"I chose risk."
Slowing the waves

By May last year, workers, many of them residents, had begun installing bamboo poles packed with brushwood along the coast. They are designed to slow water flow and trap sediment, with the goal of gradually raising the seabed and supporting mangrove growth.
When AFP journalists visited the site, workers were building an oyster-shell breakwater about 100 metres (330 feet) offshore.
Under the searing heat, men in caps pounded wooden stakes used to secure coconut-fibre bags filled with shells on an artificial shore first created with sea sand.

"This breakwater's main purpose is to lessen the impact of the wave before it can reach the community," project manager Lyana Galang told AFP, adding that the oyster-shell barriers work in concert with bamboo sediment traps.
Filipino scientist Antonio Contreras said the Philippines had long relied heavily on concrete dykes and seawalls, many undertaken without adequate study.

"We have altered the environment so much that we tend to work against nature when in fact we should work with it," Contreras told AFP, noting that some design flaws linked to corruption had cost lives.
But nature-based solutions were not a universal answer, he warned, particularly during catastrophic floods, and should complement conventional infrastructure.
Contreras said the approach in Pamarawan could be replicated elsewhere, provided local environmental conditions were carefully taken into account.
Bamboo and oyster shells also need to be sourced sustainably, he warned, as bamboo deteriorates over time and releases carbon as it decomposes.

The nature-based installations, which cover about 14 hectares along Manila Bay, cost 70 million pesos ($1.1 million), including maintenance, compared with around 90 million pesos for a concrete seawall, Mayor Natividad said.
He estimated bamboo will need to be replaced once every five years.
'Our feet are dry'
With its first phase completed in late 2025, the installation has already brought some comfort to residents.
Fisherman Edgar Javier said the breakwaters had softened waves and helped keep floodwaters at bay during typhoons and monsoon rains this year.
"This has made a huge difference for us. We can still feel the waves, but they have significantly weakened. (They're) almost nothing now," he said.
Arsenia Cabigao, 58, said flooding had previously disrupted her livelihood by submerging areas where she dried fish.
"Our feet are dry at last. They weren't before," she told AFP as she sliced small fish in a narrow Pamarawan alley.
The project's long-term effectiveness remains uncertain, with a scientific assessment due next year to determine if mangrove planting can begin, Natividad said.

Its success, he added, would become more tangible over the next decade as accumulated sediment stabilised the seabed and allowed for the growth of mangroves, which would provide another natural barrier.
Vince Dizon, head of the public works department before a recent reassignment, said he hoped the Pamarawan project could be replicated in other flood-prone areas.
"We need to study this, and learn from those who know and have already done this correctly, so we won't waste public funds again," Dizon told reporters on a visit to the island.
For residents who fear being driven from their longtime home, the ultimate test will be whether their houses remain upright when typhoons and monsoon rains strike.
"It's hard to fight water. Now we're trying to live with water," Natividad told AFP.
"We're building with nature." — Agence France-Presse

articles.title: DA: Weak peso to push up imported rice, fertilizer prices
articles.summary: Meanwhile, the Philippines' rice import volume is expected to increase by November and December in anticipation of severe El Niño

blocks.text: PRICE. A vendor sells imported and local rice at Central Market in Sta. Cruz, Manila, on May 7, 2026.
Rappler
Meanwhile, the Philippines' rice import volume is expected to increase by November and December in anticipation of severe El Niño

items: The weakening peso is expected to increase prices of imports, particularly rice and fertilizer, with effects likely felt by November.
The Philippines is facing a potential rise in rice imports due to severe El Niño, which may also reduce local rice production by up to 1 million metric tons.
Despite these challenges, the government reassures the public about food supply adequacy and its commitment to defend the peso.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The weakening peso will push up prices of imports such as rice, fertilizer, and other farm goods, Department of Agriculture (DA) spokesman Arnel de Mesa told reporters on Thursday, October 29.
“It will have an effect on imported items like rice,” said De Mesa in Filipino. De Mesa said the impact on imported rice prices may be felt “possibly by November.”
“Of course we need more peso to buy the same volume. For almost all imported items, there will be an impact.”
Among the key farm inputs that will take a hit is the country’s fertilizer needs, most of which are imported. The Philippines breached a record low of P64.17 per dollar on October 27.

Sonny Africa, executive director of Ibon Foundation, criticized the lack of government support to agriculture and local industries. Africa pointed out the dip in the DA’s proposed 2027 budget, which he described as “chronic neglect.”
The DA sought a leaner budget in 2027 – down by 8% compared to the previous year’s allocation.

“The peso is weak because the economy is weak – we need more and more dollars to import what we don’t produce, but produce less and less to export and earn dollars from,” Africa said in a social media post.

Meanwhile, higher rice imports may be expected due to severe El Niño, according to De Mesa. In 2024, an El Niño year, the Philippines reached record-high rice import volume at 4.89 million metric tons (MMT).

As of October 21, the Philippines has imported 4.37 MMT of milled rice. This is 62.66% of rice import volume expected to enter the market this year. Most of rice imports came from Vietnam, Thailand, and Myanmar.
“We can expect this to increase by November, December in anticipation of El Niño’s effect,” said De Mesa.

As rice import prices and volume are expected to increase due to a depreciating peso and the El Niño, Philippines’ local rice output may suffer as well. El Niño may cut down the country’s rice production by 900,000 to a million metric tons, according to DA projections.
Rappler’s resident economist JC Punongbayan of the UP School of Economics warned that a strong El Niño is “expected to contribute to inflation even more, on top of everything.”
Punongbayan said higher import costs would eventually “feed into transport fares, production costs, and retail prices, squeezing household purchasing power.”

In spite of these negative trends, Malacañang assured the public not to panic. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said on Wednesday, October 28, that “people can take solace in the fact that our policy towards the peso is to continue to defend the peso as hard as we possible can.”
“We have all the tools to defend the peso, we have all the means to defend the peso,” he told reporters.
The DA also cautioned the public against panicking as food supplies are “adequate” until the end of the year. – Rappler.com

articles.title: El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to Haiti to rescue four missing soldiers
articles.summary: The troops are trying to recover four military personnel who went missing in an ambush on the outskirts of the Haitian capital Port-au-Prince.

blocks.text: El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti as part of a mission to retrieve four nationals who went missing in the Caribbean country almost two weeks ago.

The "robust deployment" was communicated by El Salvador President Nayib Bukele to the Prime Minister of Haiti Alix Didier Fils-Aime earlier this week, the foreign ministry of El Salvador said in a statement on Wednesday.
Bukele said the soldiers would also assist ongoing "security efforts against gangs in Haiti", the statement continued.
Tensions between the two central American countries have escalated over the disappearance of the four air force technicians working as part of a UN-backed anti-gang organisation in Haiti.

The four soldiers with the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) were travelling back to their base in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets.
No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
The Salvadoran foreign ministry said the "large-scale operation" was "supported by various countries and international organisations".
Earlier this week, Haiti handed four bodies over to special forces claiming they belonged to those of the missing servicemen, but Bukele said they did not match.
He said one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's military uniform.
Bukele threatened last week in an X post to wipe out Haiti's gangs, saying he will replicate action he has taken in El Salvador, if they did not release the Salvadorans.
In October last year, the UN Security Council approved expanded powers for the GSF to tackle worsening gang violence in Haiti.

The multinational force has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway. More than 5,700 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, the UN says, and armed gangs control much of the capital.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in 2021.

articles.title: Prices of farm goods likely to increase due to weaker peso -- DA
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) said Thursday prices of farm goods are likely to increase as the Philippine peso reached a new historic low against the US dollar.

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 2:22pm
The Department of Agriculture (DA) said Thursday prices of farm goods are likely to increase as the Philippine peso reached a new historic low against the US dollar.
The department said the weak peso may affect the country's importation of several products, including rice and fertilizer.

"Number one, makakaapekto siya doon sa mga imported items natin. Halimbawa, sa bigas, of course, kakailanganin natin ng mas maraming piso para bumili ng the same volume. Apektado niyan. Basta karamihan ng imported items, 'yun ang magkakaroon ng impact sa atin," said DA spokesperson Arnel de Mesa in a press briefing.

(Number one, it will affect our imported items. For example, with rice, of course, we will need more pesos to buy the same volume. That will be affected. Basically, most imported items—that's what will have an impact on us.)
"Oo, lahat ng fertilizer natin imported din 'yan. May epekto rin. We need more peso to buy them," he added.
(Yes, all of our fertilizer is also imported. That has an impact, too. We need more pesos to buy them.)
The Philippine peso further breached the 64-to-one dollar level during intraday trading on Wednesday.
The local currency sank to an intraday low of P64.18:$1, weaker than the 33rd record low of P64.17:$1 seen during Tuesday's closing.
The local unit's weakness came amid the continuous spike in global crude oil prices due to the Middle East crisis.
Although there will be incoming volumes of rice, the DA said the price of rice may increase by November.
"We can expect November, December, tataas pa ito. Again, in anticipation sa potential effect ng El Niño," said De Mesa.
(We can expect that in November and December, this will go up. Again, in anticipation of the potential effect of El Niño.)
As of October 22, the DA said 4.36 million metric tons of imported rice has arrived.
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. earlier allayed concerns with the economy as the Philippine peso hit a new historic low, saying that there's no need to panic.
For its part, the DA said that the country's food supply is enough amid the weak peso.
"We have enough volume and inventory hanggang matapos ang 2026 ng mga pangunahing pagkain na nakarating na sa ating bansa, both imported and, of course, ang ating local production," said De Mesa.
(We have enough volume and inventory until the end of 2026 of key food products that have arrived in our country, both imported and, of course, our local production.)
"Again, we want to reiterate and reflect the position ng ating Pangulo na sa sektor ng agrikultura. Hindi tayo magpa-panic kasi mayroon tayong sapat na pagkain para sa lahat," he added.
(Again, we want to reiterate and reflect the position of our President in the agriculture sector. We will not panic because we have sufficient food for everyone.)
— VDV, GMA News

articles.summary: The vast majority of the decline in revenue came from weaker electronic gaming, such as eGames and eBingo. Traditional casinos also struggled, though considerably less so.

items: The Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (Pagcor) reported a 23.41% decline in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, with total revenues falling to P64.41 billion from P84.09 billion.
The decline was primarily driven by a 37.23% drop in electronic gaming revenues, while traditional casinos also faced losses, albeit smaller, with licensed casino revenues down 3.22%.

Factors contributing to the revenue decline include inflation, geopolitical tensions, and restrictions on online gambling, with Pagcor's net income plummeting 84.85% due to increased remittances to the Philippine Sports Commission.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Even gamblers appear to be feeling the squeeze of difficult economic conditions, as the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (Pagcor) reported a 23.41% decline in revenue in the first nine months of 2026.
Pagcor said on Thursday, October 29, that its total revenues fell to P64.41 billion from P84.09 billion in the same period last year.
The vast majority of the lost revenue came from weaker electronic gaming, which includes eGames and eBingo. Revenues from the segment plunged 37.23% to P27.63 billion from P44.03 billion.

Traditional casinos also struggled, although their losses were considerably smaller. Licensed casino revenues fell 3.22% to P23.10 billion, while Pagcor-operated Casino Filipino branches recorded an 8% decline to P7.28 billion.

While Pagcor’s latest announcement did not elaborate on the causes of the slowdown, the state gaming regulator had previously pointed to inflation and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East as major factors affecting the industry.

In its H1 2026 earnings report, Pagcor chairman Alejandro Tengco said the Middle East conflict had dampened consumer spending during the first quarter, with rising global fuel prices adding uncertainty.
In a separate August 10 statement, Tengco cited inflation and the geopolitical crisis, saying these had “weighed on consumer spending, particularly on discretionary activities.”

Indeed, Filipino consumers have been increasingly stretched by rising prices. Inflation accelerated to 7.2% in September with further escalations expected, while economic growth slowed to just 2.3% in the second quarter.
A May survey of 800 urban Filipinos by research firm Organic Intelligence also found that 68% were dining out less, while 42% had borrowed money for essentials such as food and transportation.

Other factors may also be contributing to weaker gambling activity to a lesser extent, including restrictions introduced in 2025 that removed direct links to online gambling platforms from electronic wallets.

Meanwhile, Pagcor’s net income plunged 84.85% to P2.17 billion from P14.32 billion. The regulator attributed the decline partly to a Supreme Court ruling requiring higher remittances to the Philippine Sports Commission, which rose to P3.01 billion from P1.80 billion.

Despite lower revenues, Pagcor said it contributed P45.28 billion to government programs and statutory obligations, including P27.61 billion to the National Treasury and P3.01 billion to the sports commission. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Cambodian police and soldiers helped guard abusive scam compounds, Amnesty alleges
articles.summary:
Survivors tell rights group that serving officers who worked as guards administered electric shocks and beatings

Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in…

blocks.text: Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compounds where thousands were forced to work in the online fraud industry, according to a report by Amnesty International.
The global rights group alleged they worked for security companies as part of a system that enabled slavery and rape in the compounds, with some guards using electric batons to keep people trapped.

“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.

Based on 151 survivor interviews, visits to 82 scam compounds and social media videos from dozens of guard accounts showing them in company uniform, the investigation said it could link illicit operations with five well-connected private security companies.

“Our findings begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny,” Callamard said.

“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”

blocks.caption: An alleged scam site in Sihanoukville, shut during a crackdown. The Cambodian authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres.  Photograph: Rebecca Ratcliffe/The Guardian

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into south-east Asia from across the world, according to the UN. In many cases, they have been lured by the promise of an office job and then forced to carry out online scams, targeting victims globally.
Among these is so-called pig butchering, a type of romance fraud where criminals build a fake relationship with a victim, slowly “fattening them up” before stealing their money.

The Amnesty report, titled Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia, alleges that a company called Leap Somnang had the largest footprint and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo, the report says.

Amnesty alleges that Leap Somnang is believed to be controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chair while also being a colonel in the armed forces. It provided photos it claimed showed him alongside Leap Somnang guards at two scamming compounds.

blocks.caption: Vacated online scam centres in Cambodia. Photograph: Ismail Kaplan/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The rights group quoted a letter from Ban Sophat denying holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an adviser to the company owner”.

“The fact that I may appear in a photograph taken at a particular location does not mean that I have knowledge of, or involvement in, the activities or operations conducted there,” it cited him as saying.
Scam site survivors have described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.
Amnesty said it had identified more than 20 members of the military and police who were seen to have an active presence at the compounds, including working openly as guards.

With annual losses estimated at about $100bn – a sum that outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region – international pressure has grown on countries such as Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar to crack down. There are signs that some parts of the industry are moving to South Asia.

In July 2025, Cambodia launched its largest-ever crackdown on scam operations, promising to wipe out the criminal networks. Authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres, and Amnesty said the industry there was now “dormant”.

blocks.caption: Leftover belongings lie scattered in a room inside a closed compound in Takeo province, Cambodia.  Photograph: Roun Ry/Reuters

blocks.text: “Even if scamming compounds are dormant, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Callamard said. “Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”

Amnesty said it presented its findings to Cambodian authorities, and cited a response from the ministry of interior stating that it had, as part of its ongoing crackdowns, already disciplined 77 police officers, prosecuted six private security guards for using stun batons illegally and detained 17 military, police, and civil officials for colluding with criminals.

Authorities had sent 3,477 suspects to court, the letter says, citing a policy of “no tolerance, no exemption, and no retreat” to ensure Cambodia did not become a “haven or operating base for transnational criminal networks”.
Amnesty said it did not receive a response from Leap Somnang.
The Guardian has contacted Cambodia’s interior ministry, Ban Sophat and Leap Somnang for comment.

articles.title: Gibo snubs China at ADMM-Plus
articles.summary: Bilateral ties between the two countries take another tense turn as Beijing sends its Manila-based defense attache to a high-level ASEAN meeting chaired by China-sanctioned Defense Secretary Gilberto…

blocks.text: CHINA REPRESENTATIVE. China Defence Attache Senior Captain Yang Lei arrives for the ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting at Mactan Expo in Cebu on October 29, 2026.
Ezra Acayan/Pool via Reuters

Bilateral ties between the two countries take another tense turn as Beijing sends its Manila-based defense attache to a high-level ASEAN meeting chaired by China-sanctioned Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.

It was but a bit of drama in what is usually a predictable ritual in any meeting under the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). As China’s representative to the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting made his way down a short red carpet walk at the Mactan Expo in Lapu-Lapu City, the camera panned to show the Philippines’ representative.
Then a handshake and a quick pause for the cameras.

What was not so routinary were the ranks of the two representatives. For China, it was the defense attaché assigned to the embassy in Manila. For the Philippines, an undersecretary who’s been representing the country in senior officials’ meetings.
Just a few minutes ago, no less than Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. welcomed representatives of ADMM’s Plus partners — including deputy ministers ranked below him — to the meeting.

It was a snapshot (or a preview, maybe) of the awkwardness and complications that can happen when a Filipino official sanctioned by Manila’s sometimes belligerent neighbor is also chairperson of a regional bloc.
There are a lot of things to unpack from the quick exchange.

First, for the first time, China sent only a defense attaché — who is based in the Philippines anyway — to represent it in ADMM, ASEAN’s premiere platform for defense diplomacy. Chinese Communist Party tabloid Global Times framed it this way: it was the “lowest-level Chinese representation at the ADMM-Plus since its inaugural session in 2010” and that, quoting analysts, the “downgraded attendance is attributable to the Philippines.”
The snub didn’t originate from Beijing.

In early September 2026, when asked about China’s participation in the ADMM-Plus, Teodoro was uncharacteristically coy when asked how he’d handle hosting his Chinese counterpart. When pressed if there was a chance they wouldn’t be invited, Teodoro played coy, too.

By mid-October 2026, Teodoro conceded that it could be awkward for China to participate in person. After all, the Chinese embassy in Manila and Beijing itself have tagged Teodoro as a problem. In June 2026, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs imposed sanctions on Teodoro and his immediate family after he supposedly “repeatedly made irresponsible remarks on China, which undermines China’s legitimate interests and sabotages China-Philippines relations.”

On October 23, or just days before defense ministers and other top officials from ASEAN and its partners were expected to fly to Cebu province for the meeting, Teodoro told a press conference that an invitation had been extended to China to participate in the meeting. The letter was signed by Undersecretary Ignacio Madriaga, who would eventually welcome the defense attaché.
On October 26, Teodoro said he didn’t know if Beijing had replied to Madriaga’s letter.

Although a country — be it an ASEAN member-state or any of its partners — must be invited by the chairman or host to participate in these multilateral events, these invitations are practically compulsory. The host country is expected to extend that invitation, regardless of bilateral issues.
By the 27th, China’s Ministry of Defense announced that Senior Captain Yang Lei, the defense attaché to Manila, would represent Beijing in Cebu.

There could be a myriad of reasons for Teodoro to skip welcoming Yang. Teodoro is, after all, ranked significantly higher than a senior captain. There are also many possible reasons for Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun to skip ADMM-Plus.
But everything is backdropped by what’s turning out to be the tensest turn yet for Philippine-China ties.

Chinese ambassador Jing Quan was summoned and widely criticized for saying the Philippines should be thankful that China does not use force in its disputes with the Philippines, as he reacted to Teodoro’s insistence that it’s Beijing that’s causing trouble in the region.

“Our functional cooperation must remain rooted in mutual respect and adherence to international law, including the United Nations Charter and the 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea. ASEAN Member States and Dialogue Partners share the same principles, such as respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, non-interference in internal affairs, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the renunciation of the threat or use of force,” said Teodoro at the opening of the meeting.

For years, of course, Teodoro has been among the loudest critics of Beijing in the Philippine government. Before China announced sanctions against him, Teodoro warned military and defense officials at the Shangrila Dialogue in Singapore that Beijing was not trustworthy in the context of South China Sea code negotiations.
China claims almost all of the South China Sea. It’s a claim that overlaps with claims of Southeast Asian countries, including the Philippines’.

For Manila, China’s claims have meant facing danger of harassment at sea in certain areas and features. For Beijing, it’s meant danger too — two of its China Coast Guard personnel died in a collision with its own warship, as both were trying to chase a Philippine Coast Guard ship. – Rappler.com

articles.title: SC seeks Senate, House comments before acting on impeachment vote threshold plea
articles.summary: The High Court instead has ordered the Senate and the House of Representatives to answer their petition first, according to an en banc resolution dated October 14.

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 1:34pm

The Senate, sitting as an Impeachment Court, resumes its hearing on Monday, August 3, 2026, on Article I of the case against Vice President Sara Duterte, which concerns the alleged misuse, questionable liquidation and systematic misappropriation of confidential funds.
Senate Social Media Unit / Wendell D. Alinea

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has held off acting on a bid by two of Vice President Sara Duterte’s Senate allies to scrap a Senate rule that lowers the votes needed to convict her by leaving out senators unable to take part in the trial.
The High Court instead has ordered the Senate and the House of Representatives to answer their petition first, according to an en banc resolution dated October 14.

The court gave the respondents a non-extendible five days from receipt of notice to file their comments. The order covers both the main petition and the accompanying request for a temporary restraining order (TRO), a status quo ante order or a writ of preliminary injunction.
The petition was filed by Sens. Robin Padilla and Bong Go.

The Senate impeachment court is named through Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero. The House is named through Speaker Faustino "Bojie" Dy III and its prosecution panel, led by Rep. Jinky Luistro (Batangas, 2nd District).
Because the court required comment without giving due course to the petition, it has yet to decide whether to take up the case at all, or whether to grant any interim relief.
Until it does, the impeachment court's September 23 ruling on counting only the votes from present and actively participating senator-judges remains in force.
In that ruling, the impeachment court held that only senators legally and factually able to take part when judgment is rendered should be counted.

Four senators are effectively left out of the vote with this ruling: Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are detained while facing plunder charges; Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, who is in hiding amid an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court, and Loren Legarda, who is on extended medical leave.

articles.title: Spain begins mourning period after deadly train crash
articles.summary:
Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims

Spain has begun three days of mourning…

blocks.text: Spain has begun three days of mourning after a high-speed rail collision – its second this year – killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.

The trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling on Wednesday morning in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to the southern region of Andalusia. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda.
Officials said on Wednesday another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition.
The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s rail network after the transport minister reported an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash.
Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight to find further victims, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes, according to Agence France-Presse.

Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, told reporters on Wednesday that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.

The Civil Guard has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.

A school in the nearby village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, is being used to allow relatives to enquire about their loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who arrived, some of them in tears.

Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said “long and hard hours” were in store because “every person will manage it in their own way”. “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated,” Garcia said.
In January, 46 people were killed and dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”.

The causes of the accident were under investigation, he added. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he said.
The first victims to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia civil agent, José Manuel Chacón.

The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media said the missing included a former minister for the People’s party and several foreigners who were likely on holiday in the country.

The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: SC orders Senate, House to comment on impeachment voting threshold petition
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has directed the Senate impeachment court and the House of Representatives to comment on a petition filed by Senators Robin Padilla and Bong Go seeking to declare null the ruling on…

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 1:15pm

The Supreme Court has directed the Senate impeachment court and the House of Representatives to comment on a petition filed by Senators Robin Padilla and Bong Go seeking to declare null the ruling on the voting threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte’s conviction.

In a resolution dated October 14, the High Court required the Senate impeachment court---represented by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and court presiding officer Francis Escudero---and the House---represented by Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III and lead prosecutor Rep. Gerville Luistro---to comment on the petition within a non-extendible period of five days.
GMA News Online has reached out to the offices of the respondents and will update this story once they respond.

In a petition for certiorari and prohibition filed earlier this month, Padilla, Go, and the Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Lakas ng Bayan (PDP-Laban) asked the SC to issue a status quo ante order or a temporary restraining order directing the Impeachment court and the House of Representatives to refrain from excluding any senator from the count of “all members of the Senate” under the Constitution.
The impeachment court earlier voted to base the “two-thirds of votes” on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."
Under the 1987 Constitution, no person shall be convicted in an impeachment trial without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.

In early September, the impeachment court invited retired Supreme Court Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno, and Hilario Davide Jr. and Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna as amici curiae or friends of the court.
Panganiban, Puno, and Davide said that the voting threshold should be based on the number of senator-judges who actively participated in the impeachment trial.

However, Azcuna, one of the framers of the 1987 Constitution, offered a different view that the two-thirds concurrence requirement should relate to the entire membership of the Senate; hence, a conviction by 16 senator-judges is needed. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Israel election results live: count of absentee ballots under way as coalition talks set to begin
articles.summary: With the final count unlikely to shift results significantly, experts say Gadi Eisenkot’s hopes of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu rest on his willingness to work with Palestinian…

blocks.text: Final ballots being tallied with results expected to show no clear winner
Hello and welcome to our continuing coverage of the Israeli election.

With 91% of votes now counted, the current results show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc projected to receive 53 seats, with the grouping of his opponent Gadi Eisenkot on 48 and the Palestinian parties on track to receive a record 19 seats.

The final tally of absentee ballots is not expected to significantly shift the results, and with no grouping managing to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israel could be in for weeks of uncertainty, as both sides try to gather enough support to form a government.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s bloc, has told Israeli media that he will meet leaders on Thursday for coalition talks. According to the Times of Israel, he will hold talks with Eisenkot, the leading opposition candidate and chair of the Yashar party, and Yair Lapid, the number-two in the opposition B’Yachad party.
This would mark the official start of coalition talks, and Golan has been the only opposition leader so far backing working with the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.

blocks.caption: Leftwing protesters blocked roads in Tel Aviv on Wednesday evening to demand a joint government of Palestinians and Jewish Israelis. Photograph: Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, voiced hope that the country could avoid a second election. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” said Herzog, who is tasked with determining which candidate to tap to form a government, urging parties to keep “an open mind”.

items: Israel’s future hangs in the balance after it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s historic elections. Indeed, Gadi Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the Arab-majority Joint List, said the Israeli public had voted for new leadership and “anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government will have to talk to us”. He told AFP that while he was willing to cooperate with an opposition-led government to unseat Netanyahu, he was not open to joining such a coalition outright. The ad hoc support of Palestinian lawmakers could enable Eisenkot to maintain a minority government, although few observers believe such an arrangement would survive for long.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee said it had received a Likud party complaint alleging that Arab parties had compromised election integrity and would examine the claims as part of its routine post-election review. Netanyahu’s party responded to partial election results showing Arab-led parties could play a king-making role in forming a new government by accusing them – without evidence – of “stealing” the election and demanding that the police and Shin Bet security service investigate the allegations.

UN rights chief Volker Turk has said that he hopes the next Israeli government will “change course massively” and respect international law. “The message is: don’t continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that’s what we have frankly seen in the current environment,” Turk told reporters in New York. He added: “Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them, and I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively.”

items: 5m agoIsrael’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition
26m agoFinal ballots being tallied with results expected to show no clear winner

blocks.text: Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition

blocks.caption: Emma Graham-Harrison

blocks.text: Emma Graham-Harrison
Hours before the final results from Israel’s elections were in, several things were clear. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority.

But most of Israel’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign in which Netanyahu painted Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state.

The self-imposed ban on a broader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections.

This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaper Israel Hayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12.

blocks.caption: Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, holds his daughter as he casts his vote in Maghar, Israel. Photograph: Rami Shlush/Reuters

blocks.text: Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population.

“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”
While Palestinian-led parties do not describe themselves as Zionist, neither do some of the ultra-Orthodox groups who are a key part of Netanyahu’s current coalition.

A survey taken as polls closed on election day showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with the Palestinian-led Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu, political psychology researcher Eran Halperin said.
But opposition leaders were silent on Wednesday, as they apparently tried to balance their desire to unseat Netanyahu with promises against working with Palestinians.

Former general Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the biggest opposition party, has not directly ruled out governing with Palestinians but laid out conditions that made it politically impossible for them to join a coalition.

Palestinians have been clearer about their priorities. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government,” Yousef Jabareen, leader of the larger Joint List, said on Wednesday. “The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”

Israel’s elections committee has said it began counting absentee ballots at 1am local time. That count is expected to last until Thursday evening, with an estimated 500,000 ballots from military personnel and diplomats to be tallied up.
They are not expected to significantly change the results.

blocks.caption: A voter casts his ballot at a school used as a polling station during Israel’s general election in Tel Aviv. Photograph: David Goldman/AP

blocks.text: Under Israeli electoral law, each voter is assigned a specific polling station and can only vote at that station. However in exceptional circumstances, some voters are allowed to cast their ballot at special polling stations they are not registered at. Among those afforded this exception are soldiers stationed at IDF bases, diplomats working abroad, prisoners and prison guards and people in hospital.
These absentee ballots are transported directly to the Knesset where they undergo a series of checks before they are counted, which is why they arrive in the final count much later.

articles.title: China stocks slip as tech weakness overshadows Fed rate decision
articles.summary: 'We are wary that investor sentiment on AI is fragile; however, we believe the risk-reward is looking more attractive again, and interest may come back towards the end of the year as investors…

blocks.text: SHANGHAI, China – China stocks slipped on Thursday, October 29, as a deepening selloff in tech shares overshadowed the Federal Reserve’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged.
At the midday break, the benchmark Shanghai Composite index lost 0.9%, while the blue-chip CSI300 index .CSI300 fell 1.2%.
Tech shares were among the main drags, with the start-up board ChiNext Composite index falling 3.6% and Shanghai’s tech-focused STAR50 index tumbling 4.2%.
CSI 5G communications, a gauge that measures the industry, plunged 6.1% in morning deals.
Robot maker Yushu Technology, also known as Unitree, slumped 4.3% after its third-quarter net profit fell despite revenue rising 70% from a year earlier in its first earnings report since listing.

“Valuations for the tech AI hardware names are now close to the historical trough and imply a major deceleration in EPS growth ahead,” said James Wang, head of China strategy at UBS Investment Bank Research.

“We are wary that investor sentiment on AI is fragile; however, we believe the risk-reward is looking more attractive again, and interest may come back towards the end of the year as investors rebuild their portfolios for the new year.”
Across the region, Asian shares gave up earlier gains as AI-related earnings announcements prompted wildly mixed responses, raising the stakes for Amazon and Intel results due later in the day.

The Fed held interest rates steady, as expected, on Wednesday, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections while it awaits further data on inflation, which the central bank said “remains elevated.”
In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng index inched up 0.1%, while the city’s tech shares fell 2%.

articles.title: ‘The more you earn, the less you keep’: readers react to the budget
articles.summary: From a young chef and a single father to business owners and a pensioner, Guardian readers reveal how John Healey’s measures will affect them

blocks.text: ‘Most people my age have written off buying a home’
Louie, 24, a chef living in London, says a lot of people have “written off the idea of even considering getting a property” in their 20s.
He is optimistic about the government’s new Your First Home scheme, which will enable people to buy a new-build property with a deposit of just 2.5%, supported by an interest-free equity loan.
But he says a smaller deposit alone will not be enough for him. “I’ve found hospitality wages to be far too volatile to even consider saving for a property,” he says.

As a result, he is studying an access course with plans to start a physiotherapy degree next year. He hopes that by the time he graduates and gains some experience, he will have a stable enough income and sufficient savings to put down a deposit.

He says the new scheme “should encourage a lot of young people to buy earlier” and adds: “We are moving in a good direction, but I’ll still save and wait until around late 20s to early 30s to start [thinking about buying], just due to how much it may cost me.”

Louie earns between £37,000 and £40,000 a year and shares a three-bedroom rented property with two friends. But rent and bills take up an increasingly large proportion of his income, leaving little room to save towards buying a home.
“I was always told that a third of your salary should go towards rent and bills, but it’s coming up to about half now, which is a little bit mental,” he says.
His landlord recently informed the household that their rent would increase by £200 a month in November.

He has managed to build up some savings. Since he was 18, he has put between 5% and 10% of his earnings into a stocks and shares investment account, and over the past year has also started making regular contributions to an Isa specifically for a house deposit.
“Nobody really wants to be spending all their money on rent,” he says. “But with the amount of money we make, you kind of have to. ”
‘I earned £126,000 last year – but still have nothing at the end of the month’

blocks.caption: Graham earned £126,000 last year but says he has virtually nothing left in the bank each month. Photograph: Graham Robinson

blocks.text: Graham Robinson is a business owner from Timperley, Greater Manchester, who runs the company KeySim. He earned £126,000 last year, but says that despite his six-figure income, he has virtually nothing left in his bank account at the end of each month.
Graham says he was “hoping for real help with the cost of employing people” from the budget. “Instead, the employment allowance stays at £10,500, while employers pick up the rising wage bill.”
He adds: “The minimum wage increase is welcome for workers, but the government gets the headline, businesses get the bill and the Treasury recoups some through tax and national insurance.”
The 45-year-old lives alone and shares care of his 10-year-old autistic son with his ex, covering all childcare costs himself.

“I know £126,000 sounds like an enormous amount of money, but after tax it works out at broadly £6,500 a month, and that really doesn’t go as far as people might think,” he says. “I don’t have expensive cars, I don’t go on extravagant holidays. I don’t really do anything particularly lavish, but at the end of the month it’s all gone.”
His mortgage payments have risen from about £900 a month to £1,300, while council tax, food, energy and other everyday expenses have also increased.
Normally earning approximately £100,000 a year, he has increasingly relied on additional dividends from his business to cover rising costs.
He is frustrated by the effective 60% income tax rate on earnings caused by the gradual withdrawal of the personal allowance on income over £100,000, which reaches zero when earnings reach £125,140.
“To put an extra £1,000 a month in my take-home pay, my salary would need to rise from £100,000 to £129,757 a year,” he says.
‘Our mortgage has increased by more than £600 a month’

blocks.caption: Helen welcomes the £100 winter payment for households like hers, but questions the methodology. Photograph: Jonathan Clements

blocks.text: Helen, 40, lives in south-west London with her husband and two children, aged eight and five. She is the main breadwinner, working in communications, while her husband runs his own architectural practice.

Her house is in council tax band D, which means she will get a £100 energy payment this winter. She welcomed the extra money, but found the way it was being distributed strange, based on bands rather than financial need.

She says the change offering self-employed people paternity pay was “great”, though now her children are older it would not benefit her family. She adds: “It was lovely to hear Dolly Parton’s book scheme mentioned, as encouraging education for all is key.”
Her family’s biggest monthly expense is their mortgage, which increased by more than £600 a month when interest rates rose. They have now fixed it until 2028.

Helen says frozen income tax thresholds are one of her biggest concerns, alongside getting the economy growing and the pressures facing small businesses. Her husband’s architectural practice is less than four years old and has struggled with the rising costs of building and a wider slowdown in construction.
“The challenge comes down to the price of energy; for example, the cost of steel, transporting materials and building homes,” she says. “It impacts everything we make, build and buy.”
‘I don’t know how people live on just the state pension’

blocks.caption: Peter thinks pensioners should pay tax if they can and backs changes to the triple lock. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

blocks.text: Peter Pillinger, 72, is a widower from South Ribble in Lancashire whose state pension makes up about half his income. He also receives a pension from his career as a Methodist minister, a small amount from his late wife’s pension and an allowance for his work as a local councillor.
He is pleased with one of the key announcements: the scrapping of standing charges on gas bills. These are fixed daily fees that households pay regardless of how much gas they use.

“My gas bill in the summer is almost entirely standing charge,” he says. “They are regressive. Putting all the costs in the unit charge will encourage people to reduce usage and to insulate their homes.”
But he wonders why it will take until at least next spring for the change to come in. He also wants to know what the government will do “for those who need higher usage for medical reasons”.

He supports the changes to the state pension triple lock and believes pensioners who can afford to pay tax should do so. “If my income is £25,000 or approaching £30,000, why should it not be taxed? If everyone else is paying tax at that level, why should I not?”
Conversely, he is concerned about those surviving on much less. “I don’t know how people live on just the state pension,” he says.
‘Flowers are one of the first things people think to cut back on’

blocks.caption: Danielle says fuel costs are affecting the price of the flowers she buys and the expense of delivering them. Photograph: Danielle

blocks.text: Danielle Walker, 37, is a self-employed florist based in Wakefield, West Yorkshire. She says rising fuel prices are squeezing her business from both sides, increasing the cost of making deliveries while also pushing up the price of the flowers she buys.
She welcomes the chancellor cancelling the planned fuel duty rise, but adds “it doesn’t undo the increases we’ve already faced or take away the pressure we’re under”.
Increasing the higher mileage rate from 25p to 35p a mile will not benefit her, she says, nor will the business rate threshold going up from £12,000 to £18,000, as she works from a studio.

Danielle has spent considerable time calculating delivery charges for different postcodes to ensure they cover her fuel costs and the time spent travelling. But she says she is increasingly having to absorb some of these costs herself.

“If I’ve quoted flowers for a wedding based on diesel being £1.40 a litre and it’s £2 by the time the wedding comes around, I’ve still got to get there. There’s only so much you can absorb for so long,” she says.
With customers already struggling financially, she feels unable to keep passing on rising costs without risking a loss of business.
“Flowers are a luxury item, and when people are feeling the pinch, they’re one of the first things people think to cut back on,” she says.
Danielle believes the government should look at the impact of fuel duty and VAT on small businesses that depend on driving, arguing that independent traders are particularly exposed to rising prices.

“Someone has to take it on the chin somewhere. I feel it’s unfair that small businesses are continually having to absorb these costs or lose customers by being honest about what delivery should cost.”
‘I am a single dad. The more you earn, the less you keep’

Jonny Roberts, 39, is a single dad from Newbury, Berkshire, with children aged 11 and eight. He works part-time at McDonald’s and as a tutor, while also studying for an online master’s degree. Between his two jobs, he works the equivalent of full-time hours. But even with support from universal credit, his income only just covers essentials.

“We had heard in the run-up [to the budget] there would be something on energy bills, and I’m sure millions of households are grateful for the extra £100 help towards that announced today,” he says. “But it was disappointing to see no announcement on whether local housing allowance [LHA] will be uprated.”

For Jonny, one of the biggest problems is the gap between the housing support available through universal credit and the reality of renting. He is entitled to the three-bedroom LHA rate, which gives him £1,200 a month towards his rent, but he pays £1,300 a month for a two-bedroom flat.
“The rent we’re paying isn’t particularly high for the area. It’s pretty much in line with the norm,” he says.
“Last year’s freeze and the cuts of prior government mean the housing element of universal credit seems to live in an alternate reality to the actual rents charged in the south of England.”
Jonny is also frustrated by the way universal credit reduces the financial rewards of taking on additional work.

For every extra pound he earns above his work allowance, his universal credit is reduced by 55p. Once income tax, national insurance and student loan repayments are taken into account, he says the amount he keeps from an additional shift can be surprisingly small.

With rent taking up the largest share of his budget, Jonny has little flexibility when other household costs rise. “I’m happy to go with less for myself to make sure I can feed all three of us,” he says.
Jonny was happy to see a “speeding up of the rollout of free breakfast clubs to an extra 2,000 schools” but adds: “It still seems a glacial pace when there are 17,000 primaries in the country.”

items: Jonny takes part in Changing Realities, a collaboration involving more than 200 parents and carers living on low incomes, researchers at the University of Glasgow and Child Poverty Action Group. The project documents families’ experiences of living on a low income and brings their voices into discussions about poverty and social security policy.

articles.title: North Korea fires around 10 ballistic missiles into sea
articles.summary: The latest ballistic missile launch comes amid rising border tensions with South Korea and uncertainty over potential nuclear talks with the US.

image.caption: South Korean television reports on North Korea's latest missile test on October 12, 2026 in SeoulImage: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea's military said.
The missiles were launched at around 12:30 p.m. local time (0330 GMT) from an area near Wonsan on North Korea's eastern coast, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement.
South Korea's military said it was strengthening surveillance and maintaining readiness for additional launches while closely sharing information with the United States and Japan.
Japan's Defense Ministry said the missiles had fallen outside the country's Exclusive Economic Zone, according to South Korea's Yonhap News Agency.
Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year, most recently launching several short-range ballistic missiles on October 12.
Thursday's launch comes amid growing tensions between the two Koreas over a border dispute that has further strained relations between Seoul and Pyongyang.
Why are tensions rising between North and South Korea?
Three South Korean soldiers were wounded on September 21 when landmines exploded in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which separates the two countries.
A joint investigation by South Korea and the United Nations concluded earlier this month that North Korea had planted the landmines south of the military demarcation line more than a year ago.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned South Korean demands for an apology as "despicable." She also rejected Seoul's offer of medical equipment.

blocks.caption: Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, has rejected South Korean demands for an apology over a landmine explosion [FILE: August 10, 2022]Image: Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last week, North Korea announced plans to resume propaganda broadcasts along the border and deploy new weapons systems in the area.
South Korea subsequently proposed talks to clarify the border and prevent accidental military clashes. Pyongyang has yet to respond.
What about potential US-North Korea nuclear talks?
The rising tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that South Korea could be sidelined in potential nuclear negotiations.

blocks.caption: US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met at the demarcation line between North and South Korea during Trump's first term in 2019 [FILE: June 30, 2019]Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: Seoul is a key Washington ally, but Trump's approach has fueled uncertainty over South Korea's role in any future talks with the North.
North Korea's previous missile launch on October 12 came a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim Jong Un this year.

articles.title: LTO vows lawful license revocation for drunk drivers
articles.summary: The Land Transportation Office (LTO) on Thursday vowed proper implementation of license revocation for drivers caught driving under the influence of alcohol.

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 12:51pm
The Land Transportation Office (LTO) on Thursday vowed proper implementation of license revocation for drivers caught driving under the influence of alcohol.

“Gusto nating matiyak na walang driver na makapagmaneho nang lasing o nasa impluwensiya ng droga nang hindi napapanagot sa batas. Pero mahalaga ring tama ang proseso ng panghuhuli dahil ang pagpapatupad ng batas ay dapat mahigpit, maayos, at walang pagkukulang,” said LTO Chief Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao.

(We want to guarantee that there will be no driver who will drive drunk or under the influence of drugs that will not be held accountable to the law. But it is important that we follow the proper processes of apprehension because the implementation of the law should be strict, orderly, and no lapses.)

The LTO previously said that it would start revoking the licenses of drunk drivers beginning November 15. With the issuance of Memorandum No. MVL-2026-242, law enforcement officers are told to strictly follow the guidelines.

“Inatasan ang mga law enforcement officers na sundin ang tamang pagkakasunod-sunod ng pagsusuri bago hulihin ang isang driver na pinaghihinalaang nagmamaneho sa ilalim ng impluwensiya ng alak,” the LTO said in a Facebook post.
(Law enforcement officers are told to follow the proper order of testing before a driver suspected of driving under the influence of alcohol is detained.)

Should the driver fail the Field Sobriety Test, then the officer will use a breath analyzer to measure the amount of alcohol in the driver’s system. The breathalyzer will not be the only test, the LTO clarified.

Other than the possible penalties of violating the Anti-Drunk and Drugged Driving Act, the LTO chief is given the power under the Land Transportation and Traffic Code to revoke the license of someone deemed by the LTO Law Enforcement Service (LES) as an “Improper Person to Operate a Motor Vehicle.”
The LES will then submit to the Investigation Division (IID) the record of every apprehension, including cases where the driver would refuse to be tested for proper action. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game
articles.summary:
Bereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the street

Bereaved…

blocks.text: Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game.

The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion.
One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.

A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.

“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed.

They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.

blocks.caption: A screengrab from the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 game released by Activision, which is made up of real news broadcast footage from Getty showing paramedics performing CPR during the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush. Composite: Youtube/Activision

blocks.text: Activision, the game’s publisher, told the Yonhap news agency that “some actual news footage included in the game’s opening cinematic was utilised as an element to convey the fictional story within the work.”
They added, “We had absolutely no intention of mentioning or treating lightly any actual tragic events, including the Itaewon tragedy.”
The Guardian has contacted Activision for comment.
The demand comes as the country marks the fourth anniversary of the crush on Thursday.
Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared it side by side with footage filmed on the night of the crowd crush.
The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced.
Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets.

The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang.
It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release.

articles.title: Bernardo says Martin Romualdez did not ask him for DPWH projects, kickbacks
articles.summary: State witness and former Public Works undersecretary Roberto Bernardo on Thursday said that Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez did not ask him for a list of infrastructure projects in exchange of…

blocks.text: FLOOD CONTROL MESS
Published October 29, 2026 12:38pm

State witness and former Public Works undersecretary Roberto Bernardo on Thursday said that Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez did not ask him for a list of infrastructure projects in exchange of commitments or kickbacks.

Bernardo made the testimony during the hearing on the bail petition of Romualdez amid a P7.4 billion plunder leveled against the latter alongside former House appropriations panel chairperson Zaldy Co, personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Sereño, and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation.

During the cross-examination conducted by Romualdez’s lawyer, Bernardo confirmed that in his six affidavits and two judicial affidavits, he did not mention that the former House speaker asked him for projects or kickback.
Asked if he never referred to Romualdez as a proponent, Bernardo answered in the affirmative.
Asked if the lawmaker never requested for list of projects from him, Bernardo said, “Yes, Ma'am. Hindi po (He did not make a request)."
“Wala pong ganun (There is no such kind),” he added.
Bernardo was also asked if he is aware of any commitment or kickback delivered to Romualdez, Bernardo said, “Wala po (None).”
He then said he mentioned Romualdez in his affidavits in the context of seeing the former Speaker during the birthday celebration of then DPWH secretary Mark Villar in September 2016.
Bernardo also admitted that he had a financial gain of 1% for every transaction involving then DPWH Bulacan First District Engineering Office District Engineer Henry Alcantara and Co.

He said that Alcantara and then DPWH National Capital Region director would provide the list of projects for proponent lawmakers for funding, and would also collect commitment fees from contractors since this will serve as kickback for proponents.
“Boss, hati na tayo sa (let's split the) 2%,” Bernardo recalled Alcantara as saying to him.
Asked by the Romualdez’s lawyer if he receives portion of the amount of a project cost, Bernardo replied, “in some cases.”
He, however, said he has no personal knowledge of the dealings between Alcantara and Co.
“Sinabi niya (Alcantara) [lang] po sa akin na nagdedeliver siya kay Zaldy Co (Alcantara told me he was making deliveries to Co),” Bernardo said.
The former DPWH undersecretary said Co only phoned him in 2021 to inquire about Alcantara.
“Sabi ko po maayos kausap si Alcantara (I vouched for Alcantara). Professional,” Bernardo said.
Turning a new leaf

Bernardo was also quizzed by Romualdez’s defense team on his statement in his judicial affidavit that he came forward about the flood control scheme because the people who have helped him before did not help him when he was grilled in the Senate inquiry on the flood control mess.
Bernardo, however, said that the people turning their backs on him was not the only reason for him to tell the truth.
“Hindi ko po masasabi na 'yun lang ang dahilan. When I learned about ghost projects, hindi ko na po kayang dalhin iyon. Kailangan matigil 'yun,” Bernardo said.
(I cannot say that people turning their backs on me was my only reason. It became such a burden for me when I learned about ghost projects. That should stop.) —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: US: Department of Homeland Security data leak exposes details of more than 40,000 employees
articles.summary: The leaked information reportedly includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of personnel across several US security agencies. This follows recent data breaches involving the FBI and the…

image.caption: DHS said it was working to ensure its employees were properly protected and would update the public 'when more information is available' [FILE: September 19, 2025]Image: Erin Hooley/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the third major US government data leak in the past month, details on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including officials involved in surveillance, intelligence and undercover operations, were released on Wednesday by a nonprofit leak website.

Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the data was obtained by an entity calling itself "Department of Peace" and provided to the group and "journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew."

DHS said in a statement that it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The agency said it would provide further updates when more information became available.
Transparency group says releasing data justified
The leaked DHS data reportedly includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of personnel from:

items: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)
Customs and Border Protection (CBP)
US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)
the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
​other DHS agencies

blocks.text: The data transparency group also provided a link to an online search tool that helps the public sift through the data.
Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the leak identifies "key personnel in DHS' ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," according to a statement on their website.
Best said the tool would "replace anonymity with accountability" and aid journalists as well as facilitate congressional oversight.
According to Reuters, the news agency called three DHS employees based on the data and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details.

DHS said in September that it was initiating a "surge in sanctuary cities," which are known to limit cooperation with federal authorities — as the Trump administration ramped up its crackdown on immigration.
The non-partisan Migration Policy Institute said in a fact sheet that the DHS has expanded its arrests and deportations over the last several months.
Third serious data breach recently
This is the third major US government data breach in recent weeks:

items: Last week, the Defense Department faced a class-action lawsuit over a breach affecting millions of current and former military personnel
In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen data of thousands of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) employees.
